channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of February 4-10, 1985 — Michael Crichton wants adventure games to make sense
item.description: February’s COMPUTE! finds the novelist building adventures around believable solutions, not magic words. Michael Crichton has a complaint familiar to anyone stranded at an adventure-game prompt: a sensible solution ought not to fail merely because the player has guessed the wrong words. In February’s COMPUTE!, the novelist discusses Amazon and argues for puzzles that answer to the logic of the situation rather than an arbitrary phrase. Also this week: Wozniak leaves daily Apple duties for a living-room video venture · Online games and conversation challenge the established services · PC-Write turns copying into a sales channel.

item.title: Week of January 28-February 3, 1985 — Commodore earnings plunge 94%; home-computer boom faces its reckoning
item.description: Quarterly profit shrinks to $3.2 million as the industry searches for its next reason to buy. Commodore’s latest figures have put a hard number on the cooling home-computer boom. Paul Richter reports in the February 1 Los Angeles Times that quarterly profit fell 94 percent to $3.2 million. Sales for the quarter ended December 31 declined 21 percent from a year earlier, to $338.7 million. Also this week: TurboTape promises disk-like loading from ordinary Commodore cassettes · The C64 becomes a six-track music studio · JTERM’s new version brings 1200-bps access to Atari bulletin-board callers.

item.title: Week of January 21-27, 1985 — Apple puts a shared laser printer at the center of the Macintosh Office
item.description: January 23 unveiling pairs a $6,995 printer with a network; March availability is promised. Apple has placed a shared laser printer at the center of its new Macintosh Office strategy. At its January 23 shareholders meeting in Cupertino, the company presented a system intended to make the Macintosh a stronger contender for office work, with AppleTalk linking desks to a common printing resource. Also this week: Atari promises Macintosh-style computing without Macintosh prices · Commodore 128 promises three computers in one · Games invite players to build the tracks, creatures and adventures.

item.title: Week of January 14-20, 1985 — Nintendo puts games at the heart of its Advanced Video System
item.description: January’s winter show offers a game machine with a home-computing ambition. Nintendo’s Advanced Video System offers a striking proposal for the living room: a sleek game unit that can be joined by an optional keyboard and tape-drive accessories. Demonstrated at the January 5–8 Winter Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, the design remains one of the month’s notable consumer-computing talking points. Also this week: Atari challenges Macintosh prices with the ST · Commodore 128 offers three paths from one keyboard · Rails West! and Questron take the long route.

item.title: Week of January 7-13, 1985 — Atari challenges Macintosh with a $400–$600 ST family
item.description: Jack Tramiel puts a new 68000 computer family against the established names; software and delivery will decide the contest. Atari is taking aim at the price of personal computing. As Winter CES closes January 8, Jack Tramiel’s company is promoting an ST family announced at $400–$600. The demonstrations began over the preceding weekend; the quoted range is an announced computer price, not a complete system already sitting on a dealer’s shelf. Also this week: Commodore answers with the C128—and a portable proposal · Nintendo proposes an Advanced Video System for America · PlayNet puts C64 board games on the telephone line.

item.title: Week of December 31, 1984-January 6, 1985 — Atari shows a $599 512K ST, challenging the high-end divide
item.description: Winter CES opens with 68000 power, GEM windows and unfinished prototypes. LAS VEGAS — Winter CES opens January 5 with Atari putting a new family of personal computers before the trade. The 512K 520ST carries an announced computer price of $599; the 128K 130ST is announced at $399. Neither figure buys a complete monitor-and-drive system. The show runs through January 8, with its opening two days falling in this week. Also this week: Commodore 128 promises three computers in one · Coleco pulls out of Adam; inventory sale points to bargains · Epyx puts young players in charge of its CES demonstrations · Commodore’s LCD portable packs office tools and a modem.

item.title: Week of December 24-30, 1984 — Ghostbusters turns the Commodore 64 into a movie franchise
item.description: December’s game reviews put a familiar movie business on the home computer. Activision’s Ghostbusters puts the Commodore 64 owner in charge of a ghost-catching franchise. Computer Gaming World’s December roundup finds the movie license well executed, with a particular eye for the machine’s graphics and sound. It is a holiday-season review, not an announcement of a Christmas-week shipment. Also this week: MSX promises a common language for incompatible home computers · A Commodore can switch the lights and watch the windows · Year-end editors still choose the under-$200 Commodore 64.

item.title: Week of December 17-23, 1984 — Enchanter brings a spellbook to the Macintosh
item.description: Infocom’s adventure rewards ingenuity as a novice confronts the sorcerer Krill. An adventure need not begin with a drawn sword. In Infocom’s Enchanter, the Circle of Enchanters sends a novice to confront the sorcerer Krill. Marc Berman’s December COMPUTE! review follows that journey on the Macintosh, where words and spells supply the action. Also this week: MSX promises a common language for home computers · Plus/4 improves BASIC but leaves C64 software behind · A modem makes the home computer social.

item.title: Week of December 10-16, 1984 — Ghostbusters turns the Commodore 64 into a paranormal franchise
item.description: Activision turns a hit film into equipment-buying strategy and audiovisual spectacle on the C64. Ghostbusters gives the Commodore 64 owner a business to run as well as ghosts to catch. Activision’s game makes the player the proprietor of a Ghostbusters franchise, bringing the film’s premise to a home-computer screen. December’s Computer Gaming World includes it among the games receiving a first look. Also this week: Tandy 1000 offers a $1,200 challenge to IBM’s junior · Plus/4’s improved BASIC runs into Commodore’s compatibility wall · Archon II: Adept trades the chessboard for elemental combat.

item.title: Week of December 3-9, 1984 — F-15 Strike Eagle brings combat flying to Atari and Commodore desktops
item.description: December’s gaming review puts Atari and Commodore pilots in a three-dimensional combat cockpit. MicroProse puts the home-computer pilot in a combat cockpit with F-15 Strike Eagle. The December Computer Gaming World review identifies Atari and Commodore 64 editions, each for one player, and credits Sid Meier and Grant Irani. Its arcade-and-strategy billing promises more than a simple shooting gallery. Also this week: Tandy 1000 challenges IBM on price and bundled software · MSX promises common software across competing home computers · A Commodore can watch the house as well as run games.

item.title: Week of November 26-December 2, 1984 — British Telecom’s Firebird wins the rights to take Elite to Z80 computers
item.description: Spectrum version promised; Amstrad conversion probable as Elite heads for Firebird’s premium line. British Telecom’s Firebird has obtained the rights to convert Acornsoft’s Elite for Z80 computers. Popular Computing Weekly reports the agreement in its November 29 issue, following an auction the previous week. The price is described as a substantial sum but is not disclosed. Also this week: Coleco and Parker Brothers retreat from the British games market · LaserJet wins a 119-printer showdown as laser output reaches the PC desk · Home bulletin boards become a social network—and an arcade · Borland sells a pop-up desk—and charges extra for an unprotected disk.

item.title: Week of November 19-25, 1984 — After Comdex, personal computing faces an IBM-shaped market
item.description: A record trade-show floor gives way to price cutting, compatibility battles and a crowded software business. The personal-computer business is taking stock after Comdex, and the mood is more restrained than the crowded aisles suggest. Reporting November 20 from Las Vegas, David F. Salisbury describes a record 1,400 exhibits at the previous week’s show, but noticeably less exuberance than a year ago. The question is no longer simply how quickly computers will sell, but which machines and publishers can survive the competition. Also this week: A $795 dish promises satellite data for the personal computer · The bulletin board becomes a neighborhood without borders · CompuServe brings more than 80 merchants into the living room · VisiCalc publisher faces merger and founders' departure.

item.title: Week of November 12-18, 1984 — Tandy 1000 brings PC compatibility home
item.description: Radio Shack’s November newcomer combines an 8088 with colorful graphics, three-voice sound and bundled DeskMate. Radio Shack has a new contender for the home-computer desk this November. The Tandy 1000 puts an Intel 8088 inside a machine intended to offer compatibility with most IBM PC software, while retaining the enhanced graphics and sound associated with the PCjr. It is a practical pitch to households that want work and play in the same cabinet. Also this week: A shopping mall arrives on the home-computer screen · KoalaPad gives PCjr owners a drawing surface in their laps · Copy protection must not punish the buyer.

item.title: Week of November 5-11, 1984 — Tandy brings a $1,199 IBM-compatible into Radio Shack
item.description: The Tandy 1000 combines PC-compatible work with color, sound and bundled DeskMate applications. Radio Shack has a new contender for the home and small-office desk this week. The Tandy 1000 enters the IBM-compatible contest at an advertised $1,199 for the original 128K machine with a 360K floppy drive. A monitor is extra: the headline price is not a complete color-display system. Also this week: The bulletin board becomes a neighborhood without boundaries · Shopping from the keyboard enters the living room · KoalaPad gives the PCjr a drawing surface · WizType turns typing practice into a cartoon duel.

item.title: Week of October 29-November 4, 1984 — Ghostbusters leads Activision’s million-dollar holiday comeback bid
item.description: Activision plans more than $1 million in holiday advertising as computer software takes a larger place in its business. Activision is putting Ghostbusters at the center of a holiday comeback bid. In the November 3 Billboard, Faye Zuckerman reports an advertising budget exceeding $1 million for the selling season. President James Levy says shipments are picking up after a slow summer, with David Crane’s newly shipped Ghostbusters and Designer’s Pencil carrying the company’s hopes for fresh hits. Also this week: The bulletin board becomes a neighborhood without borders · Shopping by modem: CompuServe’s Electronic Mall is open all night · Commodore’s Plus/4 trades game features for built-in office tools.

item.title: Week of October 22-28, 1984 — Ghostbusters Haunts the Commodore 64
item.description: Activision turns the summer film sensation into an October home-computer game, giving the game shelf this week’s biggest name. Ghostbusters is crossing from the movie theater to the Commodore 64. Release listings place Activision’s North American C64 edition on Friday, October 26; a separate catalog confirms an October 1984 C64 release. The precise Friday date rests on the release listing rather than a contemporary day-of-sale advertisement, but the game plainly belongs on this October shelf. Also this week: Commodore Puts a $300 Office in the Plus/4 · The Neighborhood Bulletin Board Takes Shape · BYTE Measures the IBM PC/AT’s 6 MHz Pace.

item.title: Week of October 15-21, 1984 — Commodore Readies the Plus/4 for the Holiday Shelf
item.description: A $300 “productivity machine” promises an office in ROM, but the C64’s immense game library will not follow it. Commodore’s Plus/4 is moving toward the holiday counter with an unusual pitch for a home computer: useful software is already inside. An October COMPUTE! hands-on report lists the machine at $300 with 64K of RAM and four integrated applications collectively called 3-Plus-1. The magazine’s reporting predates this week, so an exact October 15 launch is not established. Also this week: Archon II and Skyfox broaden Electronic Arts’ games line · Spy Hunter and Tapper arrive on home computers · A color printer for the home desk at $239 · IBM tries a second act for the PCjr.

item.title: Week of October 8-14, 1984 — Computer Games Claim the Fall Spotlight
item.description: Election simulations, adventures and strategy titles make the home computer the liveliest game machine in October’s magazine racks. Electronic Games puts the changing game market on its October cover: President Elect and Campaign ’84 turn the American campaign season into computer play. Its fall software preview ranges across strategy and adventure titles, a field the magazine now treats as the center of electronic gaming. These are October magazine features, not claims that either title was released during this particular week. Also this week: IBM Tries to Rescue the PCjr Before Christmas · Macintosh Owners Begin Looking Under the Hood · Home-Computer Forecasts Outrun the Console Market.

item.title: Week of October 1-7, 1984 — Sundog Opens a Galaxy Behind the Apple II Screen
item.description: FTL’s $40 space adventure turns icons, trade and survival into a living star map. October’s Computer Gaming World gives its gaming spotlight to Sundog: Frozen Legacy, an Apple II adventure from FTL Games of San Diego. Reviewer Ken Ryall credits Bruce Webster with a remarkably broad design: the player must supply and settle a colony, but the route runs across twelve star systems, eighteen planets and more than fifty cities. This is the magazine’s October appraisal, not a claim of a launch this week. Also this week: Game Designers Take Questions Over the Modem · Spy Hunter and Tapper Head for the Home Screen · Commodore Aims the Plus/4 at the Household Desk · Atari’s New Owner Confronts the Next Machine.

item.title: Week of September 24-30, 1984 — Lucasfilm Brings Movie-Scale Worlds to the Game Screen
item.description: Rescue on Fractalus and Ballblazer give Atari players two sharply different visions of computer play. September’s Electronic Games puts the first Lucasfilm–Atari games on its cover and asks whether filmmakers can make games worth playing. Its answer is emphatic: Rescue on Fractalus and Ballblazer bring the studio’s eye for spectacle to the Atari home-computer screen. The magazine describes a design group led by Stephen D. Arnold and Peter S. Langston, with David Fox guiding the rescue game. Also this week: Seven Cities of Gold Makes the Map the Adventure · Ultima III Packs a Whole Campaign into a Box · Educational Software Claims More of the Home Screen · The Modem Buyer Meets the Telephone Line.
